results.result: The planar covariation law of limb segment motion holds across 54 animal species (10 birds and 44 mammals) spanning body masses from 30 g to 4 tonnes, with planarity index (PV3) ranging from 0.04% to 5.3%. This kinematic synergy is proposed to be ubiquitous in terrestrial locomotion despite large differences in body size, limb configuration, and movement amplitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C37, C38, and C63 provide converging evidence from PCA analysis across all 54 species showing consistent planar covariation (Figure 3). The planarity index values (C38) demonstrate quantitatively that all species exhibit this pattern. The mass range (C2) is verified by Table 1. The inference of ubiquity (C64) is reasonable given the comprehensive sampling across diverse taxa, though the term 'ubiquitous' may be slightly overstated given the limited sampling within the broader diversity of terrestrial vertebrates.

results.result: General gait parameters varied substantially across species: stride duration ranged from 0.3 s (mouse) to 3 s (hippopotamus), trunk orientation ranged from nearly horizontal in quadrupeds (8±7°) to erect in humans (93°) and gibbons (76°), and all animals walked with each limb on the ground for more than half the gait cycle. Hindlimb stance duration was ~10% shorter than forelimb stance in quadrupeds.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C31 describe basic kinematic parameters supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and statistical analysis (paired t-test, p<0.001 for C31). These measurements establish that animals were walking (not running) and provide context for the diversity of locomotor patterns analyzed. The data are internally consistent and appropriately analyzed.

results.result: Range of motion (ROM) of limb segment elevation angles differed between birds and mammals. In mammals, hindlimb ROMs averaged 38±22° (thigh), 62±16° (shank), 71±23° (foot), while forelimb ROMs averaged 29±13° (scapula), 50±22° (upper arm), 75±20° (lower arm), 96±33° (hand). Birds showed smaller thigh ROM (~27° less, p<0.00001) but larger shank ROM (~16° more, p=0.001) compared to mammals.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C36 report ROM measurements from Figure 2 with appropriate statistical comparisons (unpaired t-tests). The differences between birds and mammals are statistically significant and biologically meaningful, reflecting different limb configurations and locomotor strategies. Sample sizes appear adequate for these comparisons.

results.result: The shape of 3D gait loops differed across limbs and taxa. Birds showed significantly wider hindlimb loops (0.54±0.11) than mammalian hindlimbs (0.26±0.06, p=0.00002). In quadrupeds, forelimb loops (FLlow: 0.49±0.11; FLupp: 0.31±0.08) were wider than hindlimb loops (p<0.005). The planar coordination of elevation angles was stronger and less variable than that of anatomical angles.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C43 describe gait loop geometry from Figure 3—figure supplement 2 with appropriate statistical tests (unpaired and paired t-tests). The comparison between elevation and anatomical angles (C39) is supported by PCA results and consistent with prior literature. The statistical comparisons are properly conducted with adequate sample sizes.

results.result: The orientation of the covariation plane (u3 vector) differed across animals due to different phase relationships between elevation angles, with higher dispersion for hindlimbs than forelimbs. Statistical analysis revealed distinct distributions: birds HL showed von-Mises Fisher distribution (k=106.9), mammals HL showed Kent distribution (k=5.7), while mammals FLupp (k=20.6) and FLlow (k=33.7) showed von Mises distributions. The u3 vectors tended to lie on a plane perpendicular to the mean u1 vector.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C50 describe the orientation and distribution of u3 vectors using appropriate spherical statistics (Figure 4). The empirical shape criterion and concentration parameters (C46-C49) properly distinguish different distribution types with significant differences (p<0.0001). The observation that u3 vectors lie on a plane perpendicular to u1 (C50) is supported by low spherical standard errors (2.4-2.7°). The statistical methods are appropriate for directional data.

results.result: The rotation of the covariation plane (α-angle) was most strongly correlated with the phase shift between foot and shank segments (Δfoot-shank: r²=0.5, p<0.0000001). Other significant correlations included limb segment length ratios for hindlimbs (Lshank/Lfoot: r²=0.45; Lthigh/Lfoot: r²=0.31) and ROM and phase shifts for forelimbs. These correlations remained significant after controlling for phylogenetic signal (Δfoot-shank: r²=0.37, p<0.00001; Δupper arm-scapula: r²=0.31, p<0.00001).
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C56 report regression analyses from Figure 5A with appropriate statistical tests. The phylogenetic correction (C55-C56) using PGLS is methodologically sound and strengthens the conclusions by accounting for non-independence due to shared evolutionary history. The correlations are moderate to strong and highly significant, though r² values indicate substantial unexplained variance remains.

results.result: Inter-stride variability analysis showed high repeatability (mean r=0.98 between averaged and individual strides) and consistent temporal patterns (hand always followed lower arm in forelimbs). Angular standard deviation of α across strides was 6-12° within species but ~180° across species, indicating that inter-species differences far exceeded intra-species variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C62 provide important validation that the observed inter-species differences (C62) are not artifacts of measurement variability. The high correlation (C58) and systematic temporal patterns (C59) support data quality. The comparison of within-species (6-12°) versus between-species (~180°) variability (C60-C62) is compelling evidence that species-specific patterns are real and substantial.

results.result: Validation analyses confirmed reliability of the markerless kinematic approach. Comparison with published data showed mean RMS difference of 5.5±3.1° and correlation of 0.94 for angular waveforms, with u3 orientation differing by only 0.7° (HL) and 0.5° (FLlow). Inter-rater reliability showed RMS difference of 3±3°, correlation of 0.99, and u3 differences of 0.8-2.5°.
results.evaluation: Claims C65, C130-C135 provide methodological validation through comparison with published data and inter-rater reliability. The small differences in u3 orientation (C132, C135) are particularly important as this is a key outcome measure. The high correlations (C131, C134) and low RMS differences (C130, C133) support the validity of the markerless approach, though some caution is warranted given the inherent limitations of manual digitization.

results.result: Hindlimb and forelimb kinematics showed systematic limb-specific differences in quadrupeds, including different covariation plane orientations, gait loop widths (FLlow wider than HL), and amplitude/phase of distal segment motion. The orientation of the covariation plane varied more for hindlimbs than forelimbs across animals, suggesting differential control and greater kinematic adaptability in hindlimbs.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C85, C91 describe consistent differences between hindlimbs and forelimbs supported by data in Figures 3-4 and citations to prior work in specific species (C82-C84). The inference of differential control (C85) is reasonable given the convergent evidence from kinematics, neurophysiology (C86-C89), and muscle activation patterns (C90). The greater hindlimb variability (C91) is clearly shown in Figure 4.

results.result: Phylogenetic analysis revealed a weak phylogenetic signal for the α-angle in hindlimbs (K=0.10, p=0.04), suggesting that the pattern of α-angles distribution is hardly dependent on phylogenetic relatedness. This indicates the planar covariation is a feature that has arisen independently multiple times during evolutionary history (convergent evolution).
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C96 report phylogenetic analysis using Blomberg's K with appropriate interpretation. The low K value (C94) despite statistical significance indicates weak phylogenetic signal, properly supporting the inference of convergent evolution (C96). However, the interpretation should be tempered by the fact that K=0.10 still indicates some phylogenetic structure, and the p=0.04 is marginal. The conclusion of convergent evolution (C96) is reasonable but somewhat speculative.

results.result: A harmonic oscillator model demonstrated that changing the foot-shank phase shift from 20° to -50° produces covariation plane rotations similar to those observed across animals. The model shows that PC1 mainly reproduces limb orientation changes while PC2 is mainly limited to limb length changes, and the plane of u3 vector rotation is similar across animals and across different human gaits.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C114 describe modeling results from Figure 6 that provide mechanistic insight into how phase shifts generate plane rotations. The model successfully reproduces the empirical pattern (C112), and the functional interpretation of PC1 and PC2 (C114) is supported by stick diagram analysis. The similarity between animal variation and human gait variation (C113) suggests common underlying principles, though this is somewhat speculative.

results.result: The authors propose that the kinematic synergy may represent a neuromechanical principle conserved in evolution to save mechanical energy, arising from both adaptation (advantage of a control law at the interface between neural commands and environment) and constraints (biomechanical coupling between limb segments). Species-specific phase relationships are suggested to be evolutionarily advantageous.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C97-C99, C117, C121-C123 present speculative interpretations about functional significance and evolutionary mechanisms. While the ubiquity of planar covariation across diverse species is consistent with these hypotheses, direct evidence for energy savings or adaptive advantage is not provided in this study. The connection to energy savings relies on prior work (C14) showing correlation with mechanical power output, but causation is not established. These remain plausible but unproven hypotheses requiring further experimental validation.

results.result: Computational analysis demonstrated that hip height and limb segment proportions impose very different constraints on angular motion across animals, with 10-fold differences in limb segment ratios (range 0.5-5). Transfer of angular patterns between disproportionate limbs produces aberrant results (e.g., trunk deformations in cheetah, unrealistic hip heights in flamingo). Despite these constraints, planar covariation holds across animals with very different limb configurations.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C22, C73-C74 use computational analysis (Figure 1) to demonstrate biomechanical constraints and the non-trivial nature of the planar covariation finding. The examples of failed transfers (C21-C22) effectively illustrate that the same angular patterns cannot be applied across species, making the observed planar covariation more remarkable. The 10-fold variation in limb ratios (C73) is substantial, strengthening the conclusion that planar covariation is robust to morphological variation (C74).

results.result: Birds form a distinct group with compact u3 orientation close to the thigh axis and characteristically wide gait loops, while primates show variable u3 orientation. These taxonomic differences suggest group-specific locomotor strategies.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 describe taxonomic patterns supported by Figures 3-4. The compact clustering of bird u3 vectors (C76, k=106.9 from C46) contrasts with primate variability (C77) and the distinctive wide loops in birds (C78). These observations are well-supported by the data, though the functional interpretation of these differences remains speculative.

results.result: The authors propose that the planar covariation law emerges from coupling of neural oscillators with limb mechanical oscillators through phase control of muscle activity. Myoelectric patterns show burst-like organization shared across species, with pulsatile activations at specific gait phases representing an energy-saving control principle. Central pattern generators may control patterns of limb segment motion rather than muscle activity directly.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C109 present a mechanistic framework linking neural control to kinematic patterns, supported by citations to prior work on muscle activation patterns (C102, C105, C107) and phase relationships (C108). However, this study does not directly measure muscle activity or neural signals, so these claims represent a theoretical framework rather than demonstrated mechanisms. The hypothesis that CPGs control segment motion rather than muscle activity (C109) is plausible but speculative and would require direct experimental testing.

results.result: The introduction establishes prior knowledge about energy-saving mechanisms in locomotion, conserved neural control patterns, and the planar covariation law previously described in humans and a few other species. The planar covariation in humans is not a trivial geometric consequence, develops with walking experience, and correlates with mechanical power output.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C19 summarize established knowledge from prior literature with appropriate citations. These claims provide essential context for the current study but do not represent new findings. The citations appear accurate and relevant, establishing the foundation for extending the planar covariation analysis to a broader range of species.

results.result: Prior work cited by the authors shows that covariation plane orientation can vary with speed in human bipedal walking but not in crawling, that limb proportions affect kinematics and energetics, and that neurophysiological differences exist between forelimb and hindlimb spinal controllers including neurotransmitter systems, cortical projections, and propriospinal linkages.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C72, C86-C90 cite prior literature to support contextual arguments about speed effects, limb proportions, and neural control. These citations appear appropriate and relevant to the discussion, though the current study does not directly test these relationships. The claims serve to interpret the current findings in light of existing knowledge.

results.result: The authors conclude that main kinematic adaptations occur in hindlimbs rather than forelimbs, implying considerable flexibility in hindlimb phase relationships. The full limb behavior can be expressed as two-degree-of-freedom planar motion plus plane rotation, with the phase shift between foot and shank representing important parametric tuning. This suggests modular control organization reducing limb coordination to two independent components.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93, C110-C111, C118-C120 synthesize the findings into a coherent framework. The greater hindlimb variability (C92, C119) is well-supported by Figure 4. The two-component description (C110, C118) follows logically from the PCA results. The importance of foot-shank phase shift (C111) is supported by the correlation analysis (C51). The inference of modular control (C118) is reasonable given the data but remains somewhat speculative regarding neural implementation.

results.result: The study demonstrates that the planar covariation law previously established for humans holds for terrestrial walking in several mammals and birds. This kinematic synergy lies at the interface between neural command signals from central pattern generators and body center of mass mechanics, providing an integrative view of limb segment motion across diverse animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C116, C124 present the main conclusions of the study. The extension of planar covariation to 54 species (C115) is well-supported by the comprehensive data. The positioning at the interface between neural control and mechanics (C116) is a reasonable interpretation given the correlations with both biomechanical parameters and known neural control patterns, though direct mechanistic evidence is limited. The integrative view (C124) is an appropriate characterization of the study's contribution.

results.result: Most recordings involved free walking in natural environments. For all animals, horizontal limb endpoint excursions were significantly larger than vertical ones, and in quadrupeds, forelimb horizontal excursions (0.95L) were significantly greater than hindlimb excursions (0.87L).
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C127 describe experimental conditions and basic kinematic measurements from Figure 2—figure supplement 2F. The natural environment recording (C125) is a strength of the study, though it introduces some uncontrolled variability. The endpoint excursion differences (C126-C127) are clearly shown in the data and represent expected patterns for walking gait.
